title_translit: Shahpurama Ananya Vaishnav Uda Dharmano Marg Drudhavyo
title_en: In Shahpura, the Path of Uda Dharma Was Firmly Established for the Exclusively Devoted Vaishnavs
translation:
Indian society was caught in blind faith, distrust, and corrupted customs and traditions. It was burning in the flames of false scriptural doctrine, brahmin-priestcraft, and empty ritualism. Padmanabh of Patan had spread the Ramkabir tradition of Gnaniji Maharaj widely. The Ramkabir tradition had begun in Kabirji's own time, but it had not yet taken shape as a distinct sect — it was only the influence of Kabirji and the spread of his knowledge and devotion. So Jivanji Maharaj established the Uda sect in Gujarat. He revealed such a path for these singularly devoted Vaishnavs that it required no austerity (tap), no pilgrimage (tirth), no yoga, no yajna, no votive offerings (manata), no ritual water-offering (arghya/anjali), no formal Vedic study (adhyayan), no fire-oblation (hom), and no ritual observance (karmakand) — only devotion was to be practiced. He gathered together the four essentials — tilak, tulsi, the name of Ram, and the company of saints — as the substance of the essence, and there was no place for the six schools of philosophy or the six branches of scripture. In marriage, without needing an auspicious hour fixed by astrology, bride and groom were wed in the manner of Sita's svayamvar in King Janak's court. Thus he practiced devotion to Vishnu.

_Uda kudya Jivana, jap tap tirath dan ||_
_Ved marag pichhe rahyu, jai malya Hari naam ||1||_
("Jivan, the Uda devotees have leapt clear of japa, austerity, pilgrimage, and charity; leaving the Vedic path behind, they have gone straight and merged into the name of Hari.")

The Uda devotees crossed over the practices of japa, tap, pilgrimage, charity, and the like, set aside the ritual observance of the Vedic path, and merged directly into the worship of God's name.

In the tradition of Uda Dharma, none of the following are accepted: lineage, ritual action, formal religious deeds, pilgrimage, vows, worldly custom, Vedic custom, the Vedic path, the worship of minor deities, or the abodes of heaven, Vaikuntha, and the like. Apart from single-minded, exclusive devotion to Ram and Krishna, there is no worship of any other god or goddess. Moreover, there is no idol worship and no brahminism. They hold no faith in sacred threads, amulets, vows, or votive bindings. The practice of the Uda devotees' Vaishnavism differs from the way ordinary Vaishnavs practice devotion. Ordinary Vaishnav people practice idol worship, ritual observance, and the worship of minor deities. But the Vaishnavs of the Uda devotees do not worship minor deities, Ganpati, or other gods and goddesses the way they do.

In this way, the Uda devotees practice pure devotion to Vishnu. Ordinary Vaishnav people worship minor deities by performing yajnas and other rites, but the Vaishnavs of the Uda devotees do not accept yajnas and such rites. They do not revere the Shaligram stone, do not perform shraddha (ancestral rites), do not honor renunciate garb (bhekh), and do not worship goddesses such as Gayatri.
